title: Google splits its 8th-gen TPU line into four with 8tx and 8i Max
subtitle: The 8tx adds hardware-enforced confidential computing on AMD EPYC hosts; the 8i Max fuses two 8i chips for long-context agentic inference.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Google announced TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max on November 9, 2026, bringing its eighth-generation TPU lineup to four systems alongside the earlier TPU 8t and 8i. The 8tx pairs TPU 8t silicon with 5th Gen AMD EPYC CPU hosts and adds hardware-level encryption for private fine-tuning and secure agent execution — AMD calls it the first cloud TPU system with hardware-enforced confidential computing. Google says select customers will be able to deploy 8tx inside their own data centers. The 8i Max combines two TPU 8i chips in one package, doubling compute, SRAM, and HBM bandwidth versus the standard 8i, with reports citing 384 GB of high-bandwidth memory. Google has not published availability dates or pricing for either system.

The split addresses two different inference problems. The 8tx is a response to regulated-industry customers — banks, hospitals, defense contractors — who cannot send plaintext data into a shared cloud TPU pool. Hardware-enforced confidential compute lets Google rent them inference capacity without the data ever being readable by the hypervisor or the operator. The 8i Max is a response to agentic workloads that need to hold large context windows and tool-call histories in memory; doubling HBM capacity and bandwidth is a more direct answer than compression tricks at the model level.

This is the first time Google has introduced four TPU systems in a single year, which signals a strategic shift from one chip per generation toward a product family optimized per workload. It mirrors what hyperscalers have been doing with CPUs for a decade — general-purpose, memory-optimized, compute-optimized — and it reflects that inference is now heterogeneous enough to need specialized silicon. The AMD EPYC pairing is notable: Google has traditionally paired its TPUs with its own Arm-based Axion CPUs, so choosing EPYC for the confidential tier is an endorsement of AMD's SEV-SNP confidential computing stack.

A note for learners: the right question when a new chip ships is not 'is it faster than Nvidia' but 'what workload is it optimized for that makes the optimization visible.' The 8tx is interesting because confidential inference is a workload the hardware actually reflects — memory encryption, attestation, isolated execution. If you can articulate the workload a chip targets, you can predict which companies will adopt it and why. That reasoning transfers cleanly from infrastructure into any build-versus-buy decision.
